analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate lower prescription drug prices and use the savings to shrink seniors' coverage gap.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2006 with 18 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have struck the part of the 2003 Medicare drug law that bars the government from negotiating directly with drug manufacturers. It gave the Secretary of Health and Human Services the same bargaining authority other federal agencies already use when they buy drugs in bulk, then required that every dollar saved be used to raise the point where Medicare drug coverage pauses (the 'donut hole' gap), so seniors would pay less out of pocket. It explicitly did not let the government force a single drug list or set prices by formula, keeping private plans in the picture. The bill died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled beneficiaries in Medicare Part D, especially those who fall into the coverage gap and pay the full cost of their prescriptions; taxpayers, since Medicare savings fund the expanded coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries stuck in the drug coverage gap

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 'non-interference' rule and directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers, with authority similar to other federal agencies that buy drugs in bulk, 'to ensure that beneficiaries... pay the lowest possible price.'

Every year, the initial coverage limit would be raised by an amount equal to the savings the Medicare actuary estimates from price negotiation, so the negotiated savings flow directly into closing the coverage gap.

The Secretary must negotiate for the government's own fallback drug plan and must join price negotiations for any covered drug at a private plan's request, while being barred from imposing a single formulary or a set price structure, so private plans and competition remain in place.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face a federal government bargaining over prices for the largest drug-buying program in the country.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on negotiated savings to fund the coverage-gap fix, and those savings are only estimates by the Medicare actuary; if negotiations produce less than hoped, the gap would close more slowly than promised.

Drug manufacturers argued that government negotiation could mean fewer drugs covered or reduced revenue for research on new medicines; the bill's ban on the Secretary imposing a formulary or price structure was designed to answer that, but it also limits how much leverage the negotiator would have.
The bill offers no other funding source for the coverage gap: if negotiations fail, seniors get nothing, so the entire benefit rests on a mechanism the pharmaceutical industry opposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward and targeted: seniors who hit the donut hole pay full price for prescriptions, and the bill directs negotiated savings straight at that gap without adding a new entitlement beyond what Medicare savings cover. The main weakness is design, not intent — savings depend on actuarial estimates and a negotiator barred from dictating formularies or prices, so the payoff could be modest. Still, the bill's cost falls on an industry with the largest single buyer in American health care on the other side of the table, which is why it was opposed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the bill on March 2, 2006, joined by 18 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and 1 Republican, Susan Collins of Maine.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
That was the last action: the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off: the ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed on the books and Medicare kept paying whatever the private plans and manufacturers agreed to, while seniors kept paying full price in the coverage gap.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats except one Republican (Susan Collins), and the bill received no committee action in a Senate controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill repeals the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices and directs the federal government to bargain with manufacturers over Part D drugs, using the savings to close seniors' coverage gap. Manufacturers would face the largest buyer in American health care negotiating prices they currently set through private plans.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D drug plans
industries.note: The bill keeps private plans and forbids the Secretary from imposing a single formulary or price structure, so the plans stay in place. But the government must negotiate prices for the public fallback plan and can join price talks at any plan's request, adding a competitor to their private bargaining.
